# Video Generation {#sec-video-generation}

An image is a single photograph; a video is a photograph that has to keep its story straight for the next few hundred frames. Video generation asks a model to sample a clip $\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times 3}$ from $p_\theta(\mathbf{V} \mid \mathbf{c})$, where the condition $\mathbf{c}$ is a text prompt, a first frame (image-to-video), a previous clip (extension), or a pose / depth / camera trajectory. Almost every modern system is a diffusion model, so this chapter assumes @sec-diffusion and only covers what the extra time axis changes: how to afford it, how to make frames agree with each other, and how to avoid training from scratch when a good image model already exists.

## What Changes When $T > 1$

**Recap of the image machinery.** Everything in @sec-diffusion carries over unchanged: the noising process, the noise- or velocity-prediction loss, DDIM-style fast sampling, classifier-free guidance on text, and latent diffusion with a frozen autoencoder. Video generators simply plug a larger tensor into the same recipe. Four things are genuinely new.

1. **Temporal consistency.** Denoise each frame independently and you get a flip-book of different dogs: identity, lighting and background flicker. The denoiser must model the *joint* distribution over frames, which means information has to flow across the time axis.
2. **Cost.** A 5 s clip at 720p and 24 FPS has $120 \times 720 \times 1280 \times 3 \approx 3.3 \times 10^8$ values. Even after a VAE with $8\times8$ spatial and $4\times$ temporal compression, that is a $30 \times 90 \times 160$ latent grid, i.e. about $4.3 \times 10^5$ positions, or roughly $10^5$ tokens after $2\times2$ patchifying. Self-attention over $10^5$ tokens is $\sim 10^{10}$ pairs per head per layer, so nearly every design choice below is a memory trick.
3. **Compression must be temporal and causal** (the video VAE, next section).
4. **Data and captions.** Clips need cuts removed, motion filtered and dense re-captioning; the data pipeline matters as much as the architecture.

**Two ways to let frames talk.** With $N = H' W'$ tokens per frame after patchifying, full 3D attention costs $O\!\left((TN)^2 d\right)$, whereas *factorised* spatial-then-temporal attention costs

$$
O\!\left(T N (N + T)\, d\right),
$$

since spatial attention mixes $N$ tokens within each of $T$ frames and temporal attention mixes $T$ tokens at each of $N$ positions. Factorisation is much cheaper but can only propagate motion indirectly (a patch that moves across the frame must hand off information over several layers); full 3D attention is expensive but models a moving object directly. @fig-latte-variants shows the family of options.

![Four ways to place spatial and temporal Transformer blocks in a video DiT: (a) interleaved spatial and temporal blocks, (b) all spatial blocks followed by all temporal blocks, (c, d) spatial and temporal attention inside one block, sequentially or in parallel with a fusion step. Figure from Latte [@ma2024latte].](/images/video/latte_variants.png){#fig-latte-variants width=90% fig-align="center"}

**Noise sharing.** If every frame starts from independent noise, the sampler has to *create* consistency from scratch. Correlating the initial noise across frames (a shared component plus a per-frame one, $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_f = \sqrt{\lambda}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{shared}} + \sqrt{1-\lambda}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}'_f$) hands the model a head start; this is the idea behind the "mixed" noise prior of PYoCo [@ge2023pyoco], and Text2Video-Zero builds its motion from the same intuition.

**Image-pretrained init with zero-init temporal layers.** The most reusable trick of the field: take a pretrained image U-Net or DiT, insert new temporal layers, and initialise them so the network is *exactly the image model* at step 0. Then train on video; the image prior is never destroyed. Concretely, a temporal block is a residual branch whose output projection starts at zero, or an explicit learned blend $\mathbf{z}_{\text{out}} = \alpha\,\mathbf{z} + (1-\alpha)\,\mathrm{Temporal}(\mathbf{z})$ with $\alpha$ initialised to 1 [@blattmann2023videoldm].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Code: a zero-initialised temporal attention block"}
```python
import torch
from torch import nn
from einops import rearrange


class TemporalAttention(nn.Module):
    """Attends across time at each spatial location; identity at init."""

    def __init__(self, dim: int, heads: int = 8):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(dim)
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(dim, heads, batch_first=True)
        self.out = nn.Linear(dim, dim)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.out.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.out.bias)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # x: (batch, time, height, width, channels)
        b, t, h, w, c = x.shape
        y = rearrange(x, "b t h w c -> (b h w) t c")  # space folded into batch
        y = self.norm(y)
        y, _ = self.attn(y, y, y, need_weights=False)
        y = rearrange(self.out(y), "(b h w) t c -> b t h w c", b=b, h=h, w=w)
        return x + y  # y == 0 at init, so the image model is unchanged
```
:::

## Video Latents and Spatiotemporal Patches

Pixel-space video diffusion is hopeless, so as in latent diffusion (@sec-diffusion, @sec-vae) we diffuse in the latent space of an autoencoder. Two video-specific points:

- **A per-frame 2D VAE is not enough.** It shrinks each frame but leaves $T$ of them, and decoding frames independently produces flicker. Video LDM therefore fine-tunes the decoder with temporal layers and a video-aware patch discriminator, so that decoded frames are mutually consistent [@blattmann2023videoldm].
- **3D (causal) video VAEs** compress space and time jointly. *Causal* means the temporal convolutions pad only at the start, so the first frame is encoded alone and an image is just a one-frame video; the same model then trains on images and videos and supports image-to-video conditioning. CogVideoX uses an $8\times8$ spatial and $4\times$ temporal compression, mapping $(4f+1)$ frames to $f+1$ latent frames [@yang2024cogvideox] (@fig-cogvideox-vae).

![The 3D causal VAE of CogVideoX: only some down/upsampling stages act on time (spatial and temporal), the others are spatial only, giving $8\times8\times4$ compression. Figure from [@yang2024cogvideox].](/images/video/cogvideox_3dvae.png){#fig-cogvideox-vae width=60% fig-align="center"}

Aggressive compression is a trade-off: it makes the denoiser cheaper but the VAE becomes the quality ceiling (fine textures, fast motion), and CogVideoX reports that going too far in joint space-time compression makes the diffusion model hard to converge.

**Spatiotemporal patches.** A DiT for video (the image DiT [@peebles2023dit] applied to video latents, with patchifying as in @sec-vit) cuts the latent into $p_t \times p_h \times p_w$ blocks, flattens each into a token, and adds positional embeddings. Because tokens are just a sequence, the same network handles different durations, resolutions and aspect ratios, as long as training uses variable-size batches. This is the central design of Sora [@openai2024sora].

![Sora-style pipeline: frames are compressed by a visual encoder into a latent volume that is cut into spacetime patches, which become a flat token sequence for the Transformer. Figure from [@openai2024sora].](/images/video/sora.png){#fig-sora-patches width=95% fig-align="center"}

## The Three Families

Families differ in how much *video* training they need, in decreasing order of cost.

### Family 1: Train from Scratch on Video

**VDM (2022)** [@ho2022vdm] is the template. A 2D image U-Net is "inflated": $3\times3$ convolutions become $1\times3\times3$ (space only), spatial attention treats frames as batch, and after each spatial attention block a *temporal attention* block mixes frames with space folded into the batch. The same network is trained jointly on images and videos (a fake single-frame video), so image data still helps.

![The VDM 3D U-Net: each block is a 4D tensor (frames, height, width, channels); spatial-only convolutions and attention are interleaved with temporal attention. Figure from [@ho2022vdm].](/images/video/video_diffusion_model.png){#fig-vdm width=85% fig-align="center"}

**Imagen Video (2022)** [@ho2022imagenvideo] attacks the cost problem with a *cascade* (the video version of cascaded diffusion in @sec-diffusion): a base model generates a tiny, low-frame-rate clip, and then alternating spatial and temporal super-resolution models (seven diffusion models in total) upsample resolution and frame rate, each conditioned on the previous stage and on a T5 text embedding. The price of cascading is that errors compound and every stage must be trained and served.

![Imagen Video cascade: text encoder, base model, then alternating temporal (TSR) and spatial (SSR) super-resolution stages. Figure adapted from [@ho2022imagenvideo].](/images/video/imagen.png){#fig-imagen-video width=85% fig-align="center"}

**Sora-style DiTs and CogVideoX (2024).** The cascade has since been replaced by a single latent diffusion model with a Transformer denoiser [@peebles2023dit]. Sora [@openai2024sora] popularised the recipe (video VAE, spacetime patches, variable resolution and duration), but its details are not public. **CogVideoX** [@yang2024cogvideox] is the best-documented open example: a 3D causal VAE, T5 text embeddings *concatenated* with video tokens into one sequence, **3D full attention** over that sequence (rather than factorised layers, because separate spatial and temporal attention made large motion hard to keep consistent), and *expert adaptive LayerNorm*: separate modulation parameters for text and vision tokens, since the two modalities have very different feature statistics.

![CogVideoX: a 3D causal VAE produces video tokens that are concatenated with text tokens and processed by expert Transformer blocks with 3D full attention and modality-specific adaptive LayerNorm. Figure from [@yang2024cogvideox].](/images/video/cogvideox_architecture.png){#fig-cogvideox width=55% fig-align="center"}

### Family 2: Fine-Tune an Image Model

Training a video model from scratch re-learns what image models already know (what a corgi looks like). The cheaper plan: inflate a pretrained text-to-image model and train mostly the temporal layers on video.

- **Make-A-Video (2022)** [@singer2022makeavideo] avoids paired text-video data altogether: a text-to-image model is extended with *pseudo-3D* $(2+1)$D layers, each pretrained 2D convolution followed by a new 1D temporal convolution (identity-initialised) and each spatial attention by a temporal attention (@fig-two-plus-one), then a frame interpolation network and spatial super-resolution are added. Motion is learned from unlabeled video, appearance and text alignment from image-text pairs.
- **Video LDM / Align Your Latents (2023)** [@blattmann2023videoldm] does the same in the latent space of Stable Diffusion: temporal layers (3D convolutions and temporal attention) are interleaved with the *frozen* spatial layers (@fig-video-ldm), blended with learned $\alpha$ as above, and the decoder is video-fine-tuned. Stable Video Diffusion [@blattmann2023svd] scales this recipe with a heavy emphasis on data curation.
- **AnimateDiff (2023)** [@guo2023animatediff] trains a *motion module* (temporal Transformer blocks with zero-initialised output projections) once on video, then plugs it into any personalised Stable Diffusion checkpoint (DreamBooth or LoRA fine-tunes) without further tuning: the style lives in the image weights, the motion in the module.

![(2+1)D layers of Make-A-Video: a 2D convolution followed by an identity-initialised 1D temporal convolution (left); spatial attention followed by temporal attention with zero-initialised projection (right). Figure from [@singer2022makeavideo].](/images/video/2d1_attention.png){#fig-two-plus-one width=95% fig-align="center"}

![Video LDM: frozen spatial layers $\theta$ interleaved with trainable temporal layers $\phi$ (3D convolution, temporal attention), mixed by a learned coefficient $\alpha_\phi$. Figure from [@blattmann2023videoldm].](/images/video/align_your_latents.png){#fig-video-ldm width=85% fig-align="center"}

The catch: the image model's spatial layers were never trained to be consistent, and a frozen backbone caps motion quality. At scale, the field moved back to training everything (Family 1).

### Family 3: Training-Free

**Text2Video-Zero (2023)** [@khachatryan2023text2videozero] uses a frozen Stable Diffusion and two inference-time tricks. (i) *Motion dynamics in the noise*: sample one latent, partially denoise it, then translate it by a different amount per frame to simulate camera motion before re-noising, so frames start correlated. (ii) *Cross-frame attention*: every frame's queries attend to the keys and values of the *first* frame, anchoring identity and background. No weights change, the clips are short and the motion is limited (mostly global translation), but it is a neat demonstration that much of "video" is attention bookkeeping.

![Text2Video-Zero: correlated latents from a translated denoised latent, and a U-Net whose self-attention is replaced by cross-frame attention to the first frame. Figure from [@khachatryan2023text2videozero].](/images/video/text2video.png){#fig-t2vzero width=90% fig-align="center"}

## Autoregressive Video Generation and World Models

Diffusion denoises the whole clip at once, so generating a minute means holding a minute in memory and committing to the ending before the beginning. The alternative is to generate causally, chunk by chunk or token by token, which gives streaming, long horizons and (crucially) *interaction*: the next frame can depend on a user action.

- **Token-based AR.** Tokenise video with a discrete tokenizer (VQ-style) and train a Transformer to predict the next token, exactly like an LLM. VideoPoet [@kondratyuk2024videopoet] does this with a MAGVIT-v2 tokenizer [@yu2024magvit2], handling text-to-video, image-to-video and stylisation in one model. The argument for this design is unification with language models; the cost is that quantisation limits visual fidelity.
- **Genie (2024)** [@bruce2024genie] is the canonical *interactive world model*. It has three parts: a spatiotemporal video tokenizer, an *unsupervised latent action model* that infers a small discrete action vocabulary between consecutive frames from unlabeled videos (so no action labels are needed), and an autoregressive dynamics model that predicts the next frame's tokens given past tokens and a latent action. At inference, the user picks a latent action and gets the next frame: a playable environment from a single image prompt. It was trained on 2D platformer videos from the internet.
- **Cosmos** [@agarwal2025cosmos] is NVIDIA's world-foundation-model platform for physical AI; it includes both diffusion-based and autoregressive world models, aimed at robotics and driving simulation.

Hybrids that chunk a diffusion model autoregressively (generate $k$ seconds, condition on the tail, repeat) are an active direction; the open question is error accumulation over long rollouts.

Other open models you may meet are Mochi 1 [@genmo2024mochi], LTX-Video [@lightricks2024ltx] (optimised for speed through a heavily compressing VAE) and the community reimplementations Open-Sora [@zheng2024opensora] and Open-Sora-Plan [@lin2024opensoraplan]. The convergence is striking: a causal 3D VAE, a Transformer over spacetime tokens, a language-model text encoder, and (in the more recent reports) flow-matching-style training objectives; what differs is data, scale and attention layout.

## Evaluation

There is no ground truth for "a corgi surfing", so evaluation is layered.

- **FVD** [@unterthiner2018fvd] is FID's video cousin: fit Gaussians to I3D features of real and generated clips and compute the Fréchet distance. It is easy to report and hard to trust: it is dominated by per-frame *content* rather than motion, so a model can improve FVD by improving frames while moving less [@ge2024fvdcontent]; it depends on clip length, resolution and the exact feature extractor; and it needs thousands of samples. Use it for comparability with older work, not as a verdict on motion.
- **VBench** [@huang2024vbench] decomposes quality into 16 dimensions, each scored by a dedicated model. They fall into video quality (subject and background consistency, temporal flickering, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic and imaging quality) and condition consistency (object class, multiple objects, human action, colour, spatial relationship, scene, appearance and temporal style, overall consistency). The decomposition exposes trade-offs, and its weakness is that dimensions can be gamed: a nearly static video scores very well on consistency and smoothness, which is why dynamic degree must be read alongside them.
- **Human preference.** Blinded side-by-side comparisons on a fixed prompt set remain the reference, especially for top models where automatic metrics saturate. Learned judges (for example VideoScore-style evaluators) try to approximate them cheaply.

## Open Problems

- **Long-range coherence.** Minutes-long narratives with persistent characters and scenes; chunked AR vs long-context DiTs.
- **Physics and causality.** Models produce plausible *textures* of physics, with objects that merge, teleport or ignore gravity; whether scale alone fixes this is unresolved.
- **Control.** Text is a poor interface for camera, motion and identity; pose, depth, trajectory and reference-image conditioning are still bolted on.
- **Cost and latency.** Tens of denoising steps over $10^5$ tokens; distillation, few-step samplers and sparse attention are needed for interactive use.
- **Evaluation.** No metric reliably measures motion quality, physical plausibility and prompt faithfulness together.

## Summary

- Video diffusion reuses image diffusion; what is new is the time axis: consistency, cost and compression.
- Cost scales with $(TN)^2$ for full 3D attention and $TN(N+T)$ for factorised spatial plus temporal attention; modern models favour joint attention with heavy VAE compression.
- Video VAEs compress space and time jointly and causally, so images are one-frame videos and decoding is flicker-free.
- Image-pretrained init with zero-initialised temporal layers preserves the image prior (Make-A-Video, Video LDM, AnimateDiff).
- Three families: from scratch (VDM, Imagen Video, Sora-style DiTs, CogVideoX), fine-tune an image model, training-free (Text2Video-Zero).
- Autoregressive and world models (VideoPoet, Genie, Cosmos) trade peak fidelity for causality, streaming and interactivity.
- FVD is content-biased; VBench is multi-dimensional but gameable; human preference is the final judge.

## Interview Questions

**Q: Why is full 3D attention costlier than factorised attention, and why do recent models use it anyway?**

With $T$ frames of $N$ tokens, full attention costs $O((TN)^2 d)$ versus $O(TN(N+T)d)$ for spatial-then-temporal layers. Factorisation propagates motion only indirectly, which hurts large movements (CogVideoX found separate attention hard to keep consistent), while one joint sequence with text tokens lets any token attend to any other. High VAE compression plus FlashAttention-style kernels and sequence parallelism make the quadratic cost bearable.

**Q: How do you turn a pretrained image diffusion model into a video model without destroying it?**

Insert temporal layers (1D convolutions or temporal attention) after the spatial ones and initialise them as the identity (zero output projection, or a learned blend $\alpha$ starting at 1). At step 0 each frame is exactly what the image model would produce; training on video then only has to learn the cross-frame dependencies, and training on images in parallel keeps the spatial prior.

**Q: Why a 3D causal VAE rather than a 2D VAE per frame?**

A per-frame VAE leaves $T$ times more latents than an image and decodes frames independently, causing flicker. A 3D VAE also compresses time (e.g. $4\times$), cutting sequence length, and its causal padding makes the first frame an image, which allows joint image-video training and image-to-video conditioning. The cost is a quality ceiling set by the VAE and harder diffusion training when compression is too aggressive.

**Q: Why is FVD a poor measure of video quality?**

It compares Gaussians fit to I3D features, which are dominated by content and appearance, so it is only weakly sensitive to temporal coherence and motion; it also depends on clip length, resolution, sample count and the feature extractor. A model that moves less but renders sharper frames can look better. Pair it with VBench dimensions (especially dynamic degree) and human preference.

**Q: What does Genie learn without action labels, and why does that matter?**

A latent action model infers a small discrete set of actions from the change between consecutive frames of unlabeled internet video; the dynamics model is then conditioned on these latent actions. This lets one learn a controllable simulator from video alone, whereas robotics datasets with action labels are tiny by comparison.

**Q: Diffusion or autoregression for video?**

Diffusion currently leads on visual fidelity and is parallel across the clip, but it generates fixed-length chunks non-causally and costs many denoising steps. Autoregression is causal (streaming, interactive, unbounded horizon, reuses LLM infrastructure) but suffers from tokenizer quantisation and error accumulation. Hybrids (chunked diffusion rollouts, AR with diffusion heads) try to get both.
